old: for Apollo had foretold him this at Pytho when he crossed the stone floor to consult the oracle
new: for Apollo's oracle at Pytho had once told him this quarrel would come
reason: "Pytho" and "crossed the stone floor" are unexplained, and the sentence gives no reason why a prophecy would make Agamemnon glad to hear his chiefs quarreling — a first-time listener has nothing to hang this on and will lose the point of the whole song.

old: There were Acroneos, Ocyalus, Elatreus, Nauteus, Prymneus, Anchialus, Eretmeus, Ponteus, Proreus, Thoon, Anabesineus, and Amphialus son of Polyneus son of Tecton.
new: There were a dozen sailors named among the competitors, including Amphialus son of Polyneus son of Tecton.
reason: Twelve unfamiliar names in a row, none of which matter again except Amphialus, is very hard to take in by ear; a listener can't retain or usefully process a list like this read aloud.

old: Philoctetes was the only man who could shoot better than I could when we Achaeans were before Troy and in practice.
new: Only Philoctetes, among the Achaean archers at Troy, could outshoot me.
reason: Philoctetes, Heracles, and Eurytus the Oechalian are all invoked with no context in the same speech; the gist (Odysseus is a great archer) survives, but each name is a small stumble for a listener with no prior familiarity.

old: we have an hereditary aptitude for accomplishments of all kinds
new: we have a hereditary aptitude for accomplishments of all kinds
reason: "An hereditary" is an old-fashioned article convention (treating a pronounced h as silent); reads as a stumble or an error to a modern ear/narrator.

old: he had had no one to wait on him ever since he left the house of Calypso
new: he had had no one to look after him since leaving Calypso's house
reason: The double "had had" is a minor tongue-tripping construction when read aloud.
